name: BME Main Building (K Building)
nameHu: BME K épület (Királyi József Műegyetem központi épülete)
intro: The K building is the central building of the Budapest University of Technology and Economics, standing on the Danube bank in Lágymányos. It was built in 1906–09 as the central building of the Royal Joseph Technical University. Alajos Hauszmann took over its design, and it carries Zsolnay ceramic elements and sculptures by Károly Senyei at the main entrance.
about: The K building (K épület) is the main building of the Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME). The university's own page gives its historical name as the central building of the Royal Joseph Technical University and its address as Műegyetem rakpart 3, on the Buda embankment of the Danube. It is a working university building, not a museum.

Its decoration is the main reason to look. BME states that the glazed ceramic elements were made at the Zsolnay factory and that the sculptures in front of the main entrance are by Károly Senyei. A 2023 article on the historic campus adds a roof of colourful Zsolnay tiles, statues about twice life-size and carved columns, and says the building dominates the embankment as seen from Szabadság Bridge.

Inside, the aula holds busts of former rectors and leading professors, among them Imre Steindl and Alajos Hauszmann. The same article describes a visitor centre in the building with exhibits such as the SMOG-1 microsatellite. A plaque in the aula commemorates the university's dead of 1956, and the building is also a place of remembrance for that year.
The building belongs to the university's Lágymányos campus, which grew up on what the article describes as a marshy outskirt with vineyards, pastures, a brickworks and a distillery.

As a university building, access to the interior depends on the university. BME has organised a guided building walk of the K building with registration; the official BME pages show whether a walk is offered.
tips: Check the official BME page for guided building walks of the K building (Épületséta) before you go: the university announces dates and registration there, and interior visits depend on those arrangements.

Look at the main entrance for the Senyei sculptures and the Zsolnay ceramic detail. The embankment side is also a good place to see the whole building against the river; the 2023 article notes the view from Szabadság Bridge.
The aula is a place of memory for the student assembly of October 1956 and holds a plaque for the university's dead. If you are let inside, keep voices low and treat it as a memorial space.
Gellért Hill and the Gellért area are nearby on the Buda bank, so the building fits easily into a day on that side of the river.
Photograph the façade from the embankment in good light; inside the building, ask a member of staff before taking pictures.

history.intro: The K building is the centrepiece of the campus that the Royal Joseph Technical University built in Lágymányos in the early twentieth century, and it has a second life in the story of 1956.

sections.heading: A university moves to Lágymányos
paragraphs: The university's roots go back to the Institutum Geometricum founded by Joseph II, where teaching began in autumn 1782. In 1871 Franz Joseph approved a new structure and the institution became the Royal Joseph Polytechnic. Before the Lágymányos campus existed, classes were held in rented buildings around the city. Győző Czigler prepared the general plan for the campus, and Hauszmann and Samu Pecz designed its buildings.

BME's page explains that planning for the Lágymányos buildings passed to Hauszmann after Czigler died, on the assignment of the ministerial adviser Albert Berzeviczy. In a memoir quoted there, Hauszmann says he kept the central building for himself while Pecz received the library and the mechanical pavilions. By his account the building was already under construction when he took over, and he mainly added the staircases to the lecture halls. Lipót Havel led the construction.

sections.heading: Built in 1906–09 under a tight budget
paragraphs: BME dates the construction of the central building to 1906–09, and the 2023 article gives 1909 as the year it was completed to Hauszmann's design. The same article says that limited funds made the building simpler than Hauszmann had intended, since he had wanted it to show the quality of Hungarian architecture of the day.

sections.heading: October 1956
paragraphs: On the evening of 22 October 1956 a student mass assembly of four to five thousand people met in the aula of the university's central building and formulated political demands. The following afternoon a silent demonstration in solidarity with Polish workers set out from the university, and that evening the Stalin statue was toppled and the fighting began.

The Hungarian government declared the university a historical memorial site on 23 October 2016. BME's 2025 commemoration report states that the K building has been on the list of Hungarian historical memorial sites since 2016, and a memorial site by the building on the embankment is wreathed each year.

name: Városmajor Park
address: Városmajor, 1122 Budapest XII (between Szilágyi Erzsébet fasor and Csaba utca)
intro: Városmajor is a historic public park in Budapest's twelfth district, laid out from 1785 on the orders of Joseph II beside the former Ördög-árok stream. It covers 100,381 square metres and holds the Sacred Heart parish church, the lower terminus of the cog railway, an outdoor stage and several monuments. A renewal of the park began in 2026.
about: Városmajor is a green space of 100,381 square metres in the twelfth district, bounded by Szilágyi Erzsébet fasor, Csaba utca, Maros utca, Városmajor utca and Ignotus utca, according to the Hungarian Electronic Library's book on the parks and gardens of Pest and Buda. The same book describes it as Budapest's first public park. The park is maintained by Főkert.

Its attractions are the quiet kind. The sources list rare trees, among them an oak brought from Paris by the actress Franciska Gaál, and monuments including a Beethoven statue, a memorial column to the architect Aladár Árkay and a statue of Hüvelyk Matyi. The Városmajori Szabadtéri Színpad, the park's outdoor stage, hosts concerts: the Hegyvidék district council's programme pages advertise one there.

The architecture around the park adds interest. The Sacred Heart parish church (Jézus Szíve templom) is a reinforced-concrete building of the early 1930s with a bell tower completed in 1936. The lower terminus of the cog railway sits at the edge of the park; the line counts as tram route 60 in the city network and climbs to Széchenyihegy.
Városmajor is a locals' park. The lower cog railway terminus, which English Wikipedia places two tram stops from Széll Kálmán tér, is at its edge, so a walk here combines easily with a ride uphill.

A renewal is under way. In March 2026 Főkert carried out a large tree-felling programme, and the two districts and the capital are planning the work in phases, including new lawn, perennials and irrigation. Telex reported the fenced area by the outdoor stage as temporarily closed while it was reworked, so check the local council's pages for the current state.
tips: Check the Hegyvidék district council's pages and the venue's own site for concerts at the Városmajori Szabadtéri Színpad; the programme and any restrictions around the stage change.
The park renewal started in 2026 and some fenced areas have been closed in phases, so expect temporary works and look for notices on site.

The cog railway terminus is on the edge of the park and the line counts as tram route 60 in the city network, so it is the easiest way to continue uphill; the Children's Railway terminus at Széchenyihegy is a walk of about 250 metres from the upper station.
The Sacred Heart church is a parish church: if you go inside, dress modestly, keep voices low and avoid disturbing services.
Széll Kálmán tér is two tram stops from the cog railway terminus, and Millenáris Park and the Buda Castle area are other Buda-side places to combine with a visit.

history.intro: Városmajor grew from a meadow beside the Ördög-árok stream into a planned public park in the 1780s, and has changed shape ever since.

sections.heading: From meadow to planned garden
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia describes the site as the floodplain of the Ördög-árok, long used as meadow and military land. According to the Hungarian Electronic Library's book, the fortress commander Henrik József Daun built a farmhouse and villa on the stream bank in 1724, and the city council bought his property when he was transferred; the book dates the purchase to 1730, while other sources say 1729. The book adds that a cemetery occupied part of the site between 1740 and 1780.

In 1785 Emperor Joseph II ordered a public park to be created here. The plans were prepared by the state architect József Tallherr, the city gardener Antal Kock began the work, and 3,000 trees were planted. The park followed the French garden style. The book gives its area on an 1786 map as 332,351 square metres and notes that it has since shrunk to about a third of its original size.

sections.heading: Decline, war and reshaping
paragraphs: In the early nineteenth century the Buda vurstli, an amusement park, moved onto the site and the park declined, with the Ördög-árok running through it as stagnant water. The stream section was vaulted over between 1917 and 1920 and the park was reconstructed, which revived it. In 1890 the area around Ignotus utca was parcelled out. In February 1945 fighting reached the park, which then served for a time as a temporary cemetery and rubbish dump.

sections.heading: Church, railway and stage
paragraphs: The cog railway terminus on the western side opened in 1874. A chapel was built to plans by Aladár Árkay in 1923–25, and the reinforced-concrete parish church followed in 1930–33, with its bell tower completed in 1936; war damage was repaired in 1965. The outdoor stage was built in 1952 and modernised in 1965. In 2026 the districts and the capital began a phased renewal of the park.

name: Dormition Cathedral (Orthodox), Petőfi tér
intro: The Dormition Cathedral stands on Petőfi tér on the Pest embankment, a neoclassical Orthodox church built by Greek and Macedo-Vlach merchants and consecrated in 1801. Its twin spires and façade were added to designs by Miklós Ybl in 1873. Today the parish belongs to the Hungarian Orthodox Eparchy of the Moscow Patriarchate.
about: The Dormition Cathedral (Istenszülő elhunyta Nagyboldogasszony-székesegyház) is an Orthodox cathedral church at Petőfi tér 2, on the Pest side of the Danube. Its congregation is the Budapest Dormition Hungarian Orthodox parish, part of the Hungarian Orthodox Eparchy of the Moscow Patriarchate. It is a different church from the Serbian Orthodox church on Szerb utca.

Visitors come for the exterior on the embankment and for the interior, whose centrepiece is the iconostasis, the carved and painted screen that divides the sanctuary from the nave. The parish's own history also names the Holy Sepulchre, a festal icon and the stasidia, the fixed seats, among the elements restored in the 1990s. Stained-glass windows were made in the late 1940s.
The church stands on Petőfi tér on the Pest embankment. According to the parish's history, services are held in Hungarian, Greek and Church Slavonic, which reflects the church's mixed past.

As a living church it is shaped by worship. Visits for sightseeing are possible outside service times on certain days according to the parish's history page, but the days and hours change, so the parish pages should be checked before you plan a visit.
tips: Check the parish website for current visiting days and service times; the parish's history page says the church can be visited outside services on certain days, and the parish publishes a worship schedule and a contact email for other requests.
Remember that it is an active church: dress modestly, keep quiet during services and ask before photographing people at prayer or the icons.
Look at the façade and the spires, which date from the 1873 work to designs by Miklós Ybl, and at the south tower, which collapsed in 1945 during the siege of Budapest.
The Pesti Vigadó, the Inner City Parish Church and the Elisabeth Bridge are all nearby, so the church fits into a Danube-bank walk.
Visit the Serbian Orthodox church on Szerb utca to see the church where the Greek merchants first worshipped, and compare the two.

history.intro: The cathedral was founded by Greek and Macedo-Vlach merchants in the late eighteenth century and has changed congregation and language over two centuries.

sections.heading: A church of the Greek and Macedo-Vlach merchants
paragraphs: According to the parish's official history, many Greek and Macedo-Vlach merchants settled in Pest in the eighteenth century and at first worshipped in the Serbian church of St George on today's Szerb utca. From 1784 the liturgy was celebrated in Greek there on every second Sunday, and in 1785 they decided to build a church of their own. In 1790 more than six hundred Greeks and Macedo-Vlachs obtained the permit, and they bought the Piarists' Danube-bank plot together with the college standing on it.

The architect was József Jung, and the founders wanted a church that would adorn the city, so the original plan was reworked twice. The church was consecrated in 1801 by the Serbian bishop of Buda, Dionisije Popović, who was of Greek origin. The iconostasis was made by the Eger wood-carver Nikolaos Ioannou Talidoros, and the icons were painted by the Viennese painter Anton Kuchelmeister. By 1809 the church was complete inside and out.

sections.heading: Ybl's spires and the damage of 1945
paragraphs: The towers had been left unfinished. In 1873 the parish commissioned the two spires and a new façade to designs by Miklós Ybl.

During the siege of Budapest in the Second World War the church was badly damaged and its south tower collapsed. Restoration began in 1946 and continued until 1949, and the stained-glass windows were made in that period. The façade was repaired in 1953, and from 1972 the exterior was restored in full except for the south tower. The interior was restored between 1991 and 1996, when the iconostasis, the festal icon, the Holy Sepulchre and the stasidia were renewed.

sections.heading: A Hungarian parish
paragraphs: The parish became so thoroughly Hungarian over a century that in 1931 it added the word Hungarian to its name, though the liturgy remained in Greek until 1949. Under the canonical jurisdiction of the Moscow Patriarchate, Hungarian came into liturgical use, and services today are held in Hungarian, Greek and Church Slavonic.

name: Elisabeth Bridge
address: Between Március 15. tér (Pest) and Döbrentei tér (Buda), Budapest V / I
intro: The Elisabeth Bridge crosses the Danube between Március 15. tér in Pest and the foot of Gellért Hill in Buda. The present steel suspension bridge, designed by Pál Sávoly, was opened to traffic on 21 November 1964 on the site of the 1903 chain bridge that German troops blew up in January 1945. Its longest span is 290 metres.
about: The Elisabeth Bridge (Erzsébet híd) is a road bridge between the Pest embankment at Március 15. tér and Döbrentei tér at the foot of Gellért Hill. According to Hungarian Wikipedia the present bridge is a steel suspension bridge with three spans: the longest is 290.0 metres, the total length is 378.6 metres and the width is 27.1 metres.

It is worth crossing on foot, because the footpaths run outside the suspension cables, which is also why the bridge is about ten metres wider than its predecessor. Hungarian Wikipedia says the decorative lighting was completed in October 2009 and officially handed over on 17 November 2009; Japan paid half of the cost and the design was by Isii Motoko.
The bridge is named after Elisabeth of Bavaria, queen consort of Hungary and widely known as Sisi. English Wikipedia says a statue of her stands in a small garden by the Buda end.

At the Pest end the bridge meets the Inner City Parish Church, described as the oldest church in Pest, with origins in the thirteenth century. On the Buda side it runs into the foot of Gellért Hill, where the Saint Gellért monument stands at Döbrentei tér and the Rácz and Rudas baths are nearby.

As a working road bridge it also affects traffic: the transport authority BKK announced the replacement of expansion joints on two Buda-side slip roads in autumn 2026, with restrictions on those slip roads.
tips: Walk across for the views: the footpaths lie outside the cables, so the Danube, Gellért Hill and the Pest embankment are in sight along the way.
Gellért Hill rises directly at the Buda end, so it is a natural place to look back at the bridge.
Check the BKK news page for road works on the Buda-side slip roads and for any diversions of bus routes near Döbrentei tér.
The Inner City Parish Church at the Pest end and the Rudas baths at the Buda end are both nearby, so the crossing can be part of a walk between them.
Photograph the bridge at dusk, when the decorative lighting is on, from the embankment or from Gellért Hill.

history.intro: There have been two Elisabeth Bridges on the same line across the Danube: a chain bridge from 1903 and the suspension bridge that replaced it in 1964.

sections.heading: The 1903 chain bridge
paragraphs: A law of 1893 ordered the bridge together with the Ferenc József Bridge, today's Szabadság Bridge. An international competition in 1894 drew 74 entries, 53 of them for this site; the first prize went to a single-span cable bridge by Julius Kübler with the Stuttgart architects Eisenlohr and Weigle, but the ministry chose a chain bridge and the prize design was not built.

Work began in spring 1898, was halted in 1902 after the abutments shifted, and was completed in autumn 1903. The bridge opened on 10 October 1903 with a main span of 290 metres, two 42-metre approach spans and a total length of 374 metres. It was named after Queen Elisabeth, who had been assassinated in Geneva.

sections.heading: Destruction in 1945
paragraphs: Retreating German forces blew up the bridge on 18 January 1945, and the Buda pylon fell into the Danube. According to Index.hu its ruined remains shaped the look of the Pest side for about fifteen years. Hungarian Wikipedia says there was much debate over restoring the old bridge or building a new one on a different line, and Pál Sávoly's design was chosen.

sections.heading: The 1964 suspension bridge
paragraphs: Construction ran from 1961 to 1964. Sávoly's design reused the original piers, and the designers studied the Mülheim bridge over the Rhine in Cologne. The bridge was due to be handed over on 7 November 1964 but was opened to traffic on 21 November, with tens of thousands of people walking across and Magyar Televízió broadcasting the event live. Before the handover it was load-tested with 80 buses and 40 trams, according to Index.hu. Decorative lighting followed in 2009.

name: Visegrád Royal Palace
intro: The Visegrád Royal Palace is the excavated and partly reconstructed remains of a medieval royal residence on the Danube, grown from a house of King Charles I and completed at the end of the fourteenth century. It is run by the King Matthias Museum, part of the Hungarian National Museum, and makes a day trip from Budapest.
about: The Royal Palace in Visegrád (Visegrádi Királyi Palota) is the site of a medieval royal residence at the foot of Castle Hill on the Danube. According to the museum, its predecessor was a house of Charles I, and the palace was developed by Louis I and completed by Mary and Sigismund at the end of the fourteenth century. It covered an area of 123 by 123 metres, with a gate tower at the middle of the street front, gardens and a Franciscan monastery alongside.

Today the palace is a museum site run by the King Matthias Museum, an affiliate of the Hungarian National Museum. Hungarian Wikipedia says the reconstructed royal residence houses exhibitions on the palace's history and reconstructed interiors, and that restoration has completed the residence and the garden. It describes Matthias-era features such as the Hercules Fountain, the Muses' Fountain and the courtyard loggia as the earliest Renaissance monuments north of the Alps. The museum's Salomon Tower also holds exhibitions.
The museum has produced a virtual 3D replica of the palace, with reconstructions of the medieval residence and photographs of the excavations.

Visegrád is a destination for a day away from Budapest rather than part of the city's neighbourhoods. The story links back to Buda: Sigismund moved the court from Visegrád to Buda between 1405 and 1408, and King Matthias later rebuilt the palace.
The museum's website carries a notice about a change to the Royal Palace's visiting arrangements, so check the official page before you travel.
tips: Check the King Matthias Museum's official site (visegradmuzeum.hu) before travelling: it carries a notice about a change to the Royal Palace's hours, so look at the current details there rather than relying on older information.
Look up current public transport and boat options to Visegrád yourself before you go; plan the return journey too.
The same museum runs the exhibition in the Salomon Tower, so you can plan the palace and the tower as one visit.
Look for the Renaissance details, such as the Hercules Fountain and the Muses' Fountain, and for the garden, which has been restored.
Wear comfortable shoes and check the weather before you go, and ask staff about photography in the reconstructed rooms.

history.intro: The Visegrád palace grew over two centuries from a royal house to a palace complex, was rebuilt by King Matthias, and then fell into ruin before it was rediscovered in the twentieth century.

sections.heading: From royal house to palace
paragraphs: In 1323 Charles I moved his seat to Visegrád and had a house built there. In 1330 Felicián Zách attacked the royal family in that house; according to the museum's exhibition text, the plot failed because the young princes' tutors blocked it. Louis I enlarged his father's house and began a chapel, but wars with Venice halted the work and the king moved to Buda. Construction resumed in the second half of the 1350s.

Louis's palace was made up of many smaller buildings over a large area, and he started a more regular palace only near the end of his life. It was completed by Mary and Sigismund of Luxembourg at the end of the fourteenth century. In 1424 Sigismund founded a Franciscan monastery attached to the south side, on the site of an older royal chapel.

sections.heading: Matthias and the ruin
paragraphs: By 1470 the palace was in poor condition. King Matthias had it rebuilt between 1476 and 1484 in late Gothic style with early Renaissance elements, and his successor Ulászló II continued the work. After the Ottoman conquest in 1544 the palace was abandoned and fell into ruin, and in the eighteenth century even the ruins were demolished.

sections.heading: Rediscovery and reconstruction
paragraphs: The first archaeological excavation on the castle grounds began in 1871 under Imre Henszlmann, and the finds went to the Hungarian National Museum. The architect János Schulek took over the work in 1927, supported by the Visegrád Castle Committee founded that year, and the royal palace was found in 1934. The war damaged the collection in 1944, and excavation resumed in 1948 under Dezső Dercsényi and Miklós Héjj.

The collection became a museum in 1953 and was named after King Matthias; in 1963 it became an official affiliate of the Hungarian National Museum. Excavation continues, and in summer 2023 a pair of gilded silver clothing clasps about 700 years old was found on the site.
